text: On the sixteenth of August, twenty twenty-one, Barcelona's new president sat down in front of the press with a folder of numbers.
What he revealed shocked even people who had been following the club's problems for years.
Debt of one point three five billion euros. A wage bill bigger than the club's entire income. A club that, on paper, was worth less than nothing.
Five years later, Barça are back in a rebuilt Camp Nou, with one of the most exciting young teams in the world. How did they get from there to here? And what did it cost?
We'll look at how the hole was dug, and at the famous levers Barça pulled to climb out of it.
Then the biggest bet of all — the new stadium — and the bill that still has to be paid.
Part one. How the hole was dug.
The story really starts in the summer of twenty seventeen. Paris Saint-Germain paid Neymar's release clause — two hundred and twenty-two million euros, still the biggest transfer in history.
Suddenly, Barça had a huge pile of cash, a hole in the team, and every club in Europe knew it.
What followed was one of the most expensive spending sprees football has ever seen.
Ousmane Dembélé, from Borussia Dortmund — around one hundred and five million euros before add-ons.
Philippe Coutinho, from Liverpool — around one hundred and twenty million, rising with add-ons towards one hundred and sixty.
Antoine Griezmann, from Atlético Madrid — one hundred and twenty million.
Three players. More money than the Neymar sale brought in. And none of them became the player Barça hoped they had bought — at least not at Barça.
But the transfer fees weren't the real killer. Wages were.
Every big signing came with a big salary. Existing stars were given new contracts with raises. Over a few seasons, the wage bill grew faster than the club's income — year after year.
Then, in March twenty twenty, the pandemic closed the stadium. For more than a year, there was almost no ticket money, no tourists in the club museum, no shop income.
A club that was already overspending suddenly lost one of its biggest sources of money.
By the summer of twenty twenty-one, the club said its wages were one hundred and three per cent of its total income.
In other words, before paying for anything else — staff, travel, the stadium, interest on loans — Barça were already losing money just by paying their players.
And La Liga's spending rules meant one thing: a club in that position can't register new contracts. That's how Barcelona lost Lionel Messi.
Part two. The levers.
In the summer of twenty twenty-two, Barça's leaders started using a word that would become famous across Europe: palancas. Levers.
The idea was simple. If the club didn't have money now, it would sell part of the money it would earn in the future.
It's a bit like selling part of your salary for the next twenty-five years in exchange for a lump sum today. It solves this year's problem. It makes every future year a little poorer.
First, Barça sold ten per cent of their La Liga television income for the next twenty-five years to an American investment firm, Sixth Street, for two hundred and seven and a half million euros.
A few weeks later, they sold another fifteen per cent to the same investor, for around four hundred million more.
Then they sold almost half of Barça Studios, the club's media and digital business, to a group of buyers. Some of those deals later ran into serious problems with payments.
Because of how football accounting works, much of this money could be counted as profit in a single year. And that profit opened room under La Liga's spending limit.
And Barça used that room immediately. That summer, they signed Robert Lewandowski, Raphinha and Jules Koundé.
Franck Kessié and Andreas Christensen arrived on free transfers.
Critics called it reckless — spending money borrowed from the future on a squad that needed rebuilding. Supporters called it necessary.
The next season, Barça won La Liga. For now, at least, the gamble had paid off on the pitch.

There was also new money coming in, not just future money being sold. In twenty twenty-two, Spotify became the club's main sponsor, with its name on the shirt and on the stadium, in a deal reported at around two hundred and eighty million euros.
For the first time in its history, the Camp Nou had a sponsor's name in front of it. For some members, that was a line the club should never have crossed. For the accountants, it was a lifeline.
Part three. The stadium bet.
At the same time, Barça took on the biggest project in their history: rebuilding the Camp Nou, while carrying all that debt. The financing for the works was put at well over a billion euros.
In the summer of twenty twenty-three, the team moved out to the Olympic stadium on Montjuïc — smaller, further from the city centre, and with less income from every match.
The return was delayed again and again. Barça finally came home in November twenty twenty-five, to a stadium that was still only partly finished.
The bet is this: a modern stadium, with more premium seats, hospitality and events, will earn far more than the old one ever did — enough to pay back the loans and much more.
If the bet works, Barça will have one of the highest matchday incomes in world football, and the room to compete with the richest clubs again.
If it doesn't, the club faces years of repayments, with less TV money than its rivals because of the levers — and the spending limits that come with that.
Part four. The bill.
Here's what the escape cost. For twenty-five years, a quarter of Barça's La Liga television money goes to someone else.

Again and again, the club has signed players and then struggled to register them in time — the most famous case being Dani Olmo, whose registration became a months-long legal and financial saga in twenty twenty-four and twenty-five.
And there are the players who left because there was no room for them. Messi was the first, and the biggest. He was not the last.
Part five. The twist.
Here's the part nobody planned. Because Barça couldn't afford to buy stars, they had to trust their academy.
Gavi. Balde. Fermín López. Pau Cubarsí. Marc Casadó. And Lamine Yamal. Players who cost nothing in transfer fees became the heart of the team.
It's a strange irony. The money crisis that pushed out the greatest player in the club's history also opened the door for the next generation — and for one teenager who might become the next one.
So has Barça escaped the hole? The honest answer is: partly.
The club survived a crisis that could have broken it. It has a new stadium, a new kit deal reported as the biggest in its history, and a team built for the next decade.
But it is still paying for the decisions of twenty seventeen to twenty twenty-one — and it will be for a long time.
The real test isn't whether Barça can survive. It's whether they can stay disciplined when the money finally starts flowing again.
So what do you think — were the levers worth it? Tell me in the comments. I read them all.
And if you want to see what might have happened if Barça had found the money for Messi in twenty twenty-one, watch this next.
